title: Ang 1360–1364: Gatha, Funhe, Chaubole
hookLine: short, dense poems of Guru Arjan
tomorrow: a saint calls himself the worst of all, and the Lord's dog. why?

cards: A text that says only 'outside' can hold a whole evening: I made it, I'm here, come down. Short can be full.

A few pages after the old style, on ang 1361, Guru Arjan writes small verses called Funhe, and each one ends on the same word: harihaan, a call to the Lord. Before them comes the Gatha; after them, the Chaubole.
Three tiny forms on a handful of pages. What does short do that long can't?

teach.b: Start with the Funhe. Each verse paints one picture, of longing for the Beloved, of the world's pull, of the company of the holy, and then the last word turns the picture into a call: harihaan. No explanation follows.
The Gatha, before them, works the same way in another old style: the body that passes, the Name that lasts, said once and left. Then the Chaubole.
These verses are addressed to people by name, as if handed to them, and one of them, in paraphrase, says: if this love could be bought with money, the rich would never go without it.
That's the whole verse's argument, in a single picture.
Love isn't for sale, and the poem doesn't spend a word more proving it. So what does short do? It makes you finish the thought.
A long hymn walks you all the way.

teach.h: THE STOP IS PART OF IT.
teach.b: A dense verse hands you the picture and stops, and the stopping is part of the teaching, because the listener has to carry the rest.
Guru Arjan wrote long hymns too. Here he shows the other skill: knowing exactly where to stop.

how: The Gatha, Funhe and Chaubole are read in the closing pages of the Granth; in kirtan the Funhe are sometimes sung with harihaan drawn out at the end of each verse.

games.q: Guru Arjan's small forms — tap the pairs.

s: short verses in the Granth are lighter than the long hymns
the Funhe and Chaubole pack a whole teaching into one picture and a stop.
each verse of the Funhe ends on the word harihaan
the same word closes each one, turning the picture into a call.
the Chaubole say love goes to whoever can afford it
the opposite: if love could be bought, the rich would never go without it.

games.q: your cousin's wedding speech is ten minutes of thank-yous, and the room is drifting. she asks you to help. what do the Funhe suggest?
o: keep one true picture of the couple, then stop and let it land.
keep every name; leaving anyone out is rude, so length is kinder.
cut it to 'congrats, love you both,' and sit right back down.
games.why: the Funhe aren't bare; they're full. one picture, a word that turns it toward the One, and a stop. short for its own sake misses it; dense is the point.

practice: Write one line by hand about something that matters to you this week. Cross out every word that isn't carrying weight, until only the picture is left. Then let the sit hold that last version.
